title: Foundations I: modularity theory – information hiding, dependency graphs and Martin's metrics
description: Why Parnas's information hiding works, what a dependency graph can prove, why a strict layering rule rules out cycles, and what Martin's instability and abstractness metrics say about the real Library Loans code.
outcome: You can model a code base as a directed graph, prove that strict layering implies acyclicity (and the converse), compute Ca, Ce, I, A and Dn from source code, and critique what these numbers can and cannot tell you.
environment: Python 3.12 standard library only (ast, random, math). No packages to install.
estimatedTime: 4-6 hours (reading 1 h, lecture 1.5 h, lab 0.5 h, problem set 2-3 h)
prerequisites: Discrete mathematics: directed graphs, paths, cycles, strongly connected components
Proof techniques: proof by contradiction, induction on path length
Coordinate geometry: distance from a point to a line
Lessons 2, 3 and 7 (the Library Loans code that is analysed)
learningObjectives: Explain Parnas's information-hiding criterion and contrast it with decomposition by processing steps, using the KWIC example.
Prove that a strict layering rule implies an acyclic dependency graph, and prove the converse with a longest-path layering.
Derive the distance of a component from Martin's main sequence and compute Ca, Ce, I, A and Dn for real modules.
Analyze a real dependency graph for cycles and strongly connected components, and evaluate whether a detected cycle is architectural.
Critique the use of coupling metrics as quality predictors in the light of the empirical evidence (size confounding, network measures).

glossary.meaning: Parnas's criterion: each module hides one design decision that is likely to change behind an interface that does not reveal it.
Directed graph G = (V, E); an edge u → v means module u depends on (imports, calls) module v.
A function ℓ: V → ℕ with ℓ(u) > ℓ(v) for every edge u → v: every dependency points to a strictly lower layer.
A maximal set of modules in which every module can reach every other; a cycle lives inside one SCC.
The graph whose nodes are the SCCs of G; it is always acyclic.
Afferent couplings (who depends on me) / efferent couplings (whom I depend on) – Martin 1994.
Ce / (Ca + Ce): 0 = maximally stable (hard to change), 1 = maximally unstable.
A = abstract classes / all classes; Dn = |A + I − 1|, the normalised distance from the main sequence A + I = 1.

conceptSummary: A module hides a decision; a dependency graph makes 'who must change' computable. Strict layering ⇔ acyclic, cycles collapse into SCCs, and Martin's I/A/Dn turn imports into numbers – useful signals, weak evidence on their own.

theorems.name: T23.1 Strict layering ⇔ acyclic dependency graph
theorems.statement: Let G = (V, E) be a finite dependency graph. (a) If G has a strict layering ℓ (ℓ(u) > ℓ(v) for every edge u → v), then G has no cycle. (b) Conversely, every finite acyclic G has a strict layering, for example ℓ(v) = length of the longest path that starts at v.
theorems.proof:
(a) Suppose G had a cycle v₀ → v₁ → … → v_k = v₀ with k ≥ 1. Applying the layering rule to each edge gives ℓ(v₀) > ℓ(v₁) > … > ℓ(v_k) = ℓ(v₀), so ℓ(v₀) > ℓ(v₀), a contradiction. Hence no cycle exists.

(b) Let G be finite and acyclic. A path cannot repeat a vertex (the repeated part would be a cycle), so every path has length ≤ |V| − 1 and ℓ(v) = max{length of a path starting at v} is a well-defined natural number (0 for a sink). Take an edge u → v and a longest path P from v. Prefixing u gives a walk u → P; u is not on P (otherwise u → v ⇝ u would be a cycle), so it is a path of length ℓ(v) + 1. Therefore ℓ(u) ≥ ℓ(v) + 1 > ℓ(v). ∎

Corollary: a rule that also allows dependencies *within* a layer (ℓ(u) ≥ ℓ(v)) does not guarantee acyclicity – two modules of the same layer may import each other. Strictness is what the proof uses.

theorems.name: T23.2 The condensation of any dependency graph is acyclic
theorems.statement: Partition V into strongly connected components (SCCs). The condensation G*, with one node per SCC and an edge C → D (C ≠ D) whenever some u ∈ C depends on some v ∈ D, is acyclic. Hence every cycle lies inside one SCC, and by T23.1(b) the SCCs can always be strictly layered.
theorems.proof:
Suppose G* had a cycle C₀ → C₁ → … → C_k = C₀ with C₀ ≠ C₁. For an edge Cᵢ → Cᵢ₊₁ there are u ∈ Cᵢ, v ∈ Cᵢ₊₁ with u → v; because each SCC is strongly connected, every x ∈ Cᵢ reaches u, and v reaches every y ∈ Cᵢ₊₁. So every node of Cᵢ reaches every node of Cᵢ₊₁. Chaining around the cycle, every node of C₀ reaches every node of C₁ and vice versa, so C₀ ∪ C₁ is strongly connected – contradicting the maximality of the SCC C₀. ∎

Design reading: modules in one non-trivial SCC must be understood, tested and released together; for change propagation they behave as one module. Tarjan's algorithm finds all SCCs in time linear in |V| + |E|.

theorems.name: T23.3 Martin's metrics: ranges and the distance to the main sequence
theorems.statement: For a component with Ca + Ce > 0, Nc classes of which Na are abstract: I = Ce / (Ca + Ce) ∈ [0, 1], A = Na / Nc ∈ [0, 1], and the Euclidean distance from the point (I, A) to the main sequence A + I = 1 is |A + I − 1| / √2 ∈ [0, 1/√2]. Martin's normalised distance is Dn = |A + I − 1| ∈ [0, 1].
theorems.proof:
Ranges: 0 ≤ Ce ≤ Ca + Ce and 0 ≤ Na ≤ Nc, so both ratios lie in [0, 1]. Distance: the distance from (x₀, y₀) to the line ax + by + c = 0 is |ax₀ + by₀ + c| / √(a² + b²) (project the point onto the unit normal (a, b)/√(a² + b²)). With x = I, y = A, a = b = 1, c = −1 this is |I + A − 1| / √2. On the unit square |I + A − 1| ≤ 1, with equality only at the corners (0, 0) ('zone of pain': stable and concrete) and (1, 1) ('zone of uselessness': abstract and unused). ∎

Note on the source: Martin's 1994 paper prints the distance as |(A + I − 1) ÷ 2| but states its range as [0, ~0.707], which matches division by √2; the check computes the distance by brute force and confirms the √2 form. A module with no classes has A undefined; the lab uses the convention A = 0 (concrete).

problemSet.problem: Prove T23.1(a) in your own words: if every dependency of a code base points to a strictly lower layer, the dependency graph contains no cycle.
problemSet.solution: Assume a cycle v₀ → … → v_k = v₀ (k ≥ 1). Each edge strictly decreases the layer, so ℓ(v₀) > ℓ(v₁) > … > ℓ(v_k). Since v_k = v₀ this gives ℓ(v₀) > ℓ(v₀), impossible. So no cycle exists. Marks: set-up of the cycle (1), use of strictness on every edge (2), the contradiction (1), conclusion (1).

problemSet.problem: (a) Prove that every finite acyclic dependency graph admits a strict layering. (b) Show by a two-module example that the rule 'depend only on your own layer or lower' does not guarantee acyclicity.
problemSet.solution: (a) Define ℓ(v) as the length of a longest path starting at v; in a finite acyclic graph paths cannot repeat vertices, so lengths are bounded by |V| − 1 and ℓ is well defined. For an edge u → v, prefix u to a longest path from v; u is not on that path (else there would be a cycle through u), so ℓ(u) ≥ ℓ(v) + 1 > ℓ(v). (b) Put modules a and b in the same layer with a → b and b → a: both edges satisfy ℓ(a) ≥ ℓ(b) and ℓ(b) ≥ ℓ(a), yet a → b → a is a cycle. The lab confirms the pattern at scale: with same-layer edges allowed, 1659 of 2000 random graphs had a cycle; with strict layering 0 of 2000.

problemSet.problem: A component has 3 afferent and 1 efferent couplings and contains 4 classes, 1 of them abstract. Compute I, A and Dn, and say which zone it is closest to.
problemSet.solution: I = Ce / (Ca + Ce) = 1 / 4; A = 1 / 4; Dn = |A + I − 1| = |0.5 − 1|. Result: I = 0.25, A = 0.25, Dn = 0.50. It lies below the main sequence towards (0, 0), the 'zone of pain': fairly stable but mostly concrete, so changes to it are both likely to be needed and expensive. Recomputed by research/l500_checks.py.

problemSet.problem: In the L200 #7 hexagonal lab, driving_cli and driving_http import only exception classes from domain. A refactor moves the four exception classes (LoanError, BookAlreadyOnLoan, LoanLimitReached, LoanNotFound) into ports, so both driving adapters import ports instead of domain. Using the lab's measured graph (domain: 6 classes, Ca 5, Ce 1; ports: 2 abstract Protocols, Ca 1, Ce 0), recompute I, A and Dn for domain and ports and the mean Dn over all 7 modules. Is the refactor an improvement by Martin's measure?
problemSet.solution: After the move: domain keeps Loan and LoanService (2 concrete classes, A = 0); Ca = 3 (app, driven_memory, driven_sqlite), Ce = 1 (ports), I = 1/4 = 0.25, Dn = |0 + 0.25 − 1| = 0.75. ports has 6 classes, 2 abstract, A = 1/3; Ca = 3 (domain and the two driving adapters), Ce = 0, I = 0, Dn = |1/3 + 0 − 1| = 2/3. The other modules are unchanged. Result: domain I = 0.25, Dn = 0.75; ports A = 0.33, Dn = 0.67; mean Dn 0.405 -> 0.488. The domain moves slightly towards the main sequence but ports leaves it (concrete exceptions in a stable package), so the average gets worse. Lesson: a metric judges one dimension; a better move would be a separate stable 'errors' contract or translating errors at the port. Recomputed from the real graph by research/l500_checks.py.

problemSet.problem: Read with its `if __name__ == "__main__":` blocks, the hexagonal lab has the cycle {app, driving_cli}; without them it is acyclic. Is this an architectural cycle? Argue both sides and propose a fix that a fitness function can keep.
problemSet.solution: For 'not architectural': the import is executed only when driving_cli runs as a script, after app is fully loaded, so there is no import-time cycle and the library code is layered (T23.1 check). For 'architectural': the source text couples an adapter to the composition root; a static tool that reads every import (and a reader) sees a cycle, and the CLI cannot be reused without app. Fix: move the CLI entry point into the composition root (e.g. `python app.py cli …`) or a separate `main_cli.py` that imports both, so adapters never import app. Keep it with a fitness function that builds the graph *including* __main__ blocks and asserts the condensation has only singleton SCCs (labs/L500/23-modularity-theory/modularity.py, include_main=True).

problemSet.problem: Nine modules are placed in three layers of sizes 2, 3 and 4. How many directed dependency edges between distinct modules are possible in principle, and how many does a strict layering rule allow?
problemSet.solution: Possible ordered pairs: 9 × 8 = 72. Strict layering allows only edges from a higher to a strictly lower layer: 2·3 + 2·4 + 3·4 = 6 + 8 + 12 = 26 (direction fixed by the layer order). Result: 72 possible edges, 26 allowed. The rule removes all same-layer and upward edges – exactly the edges that can close a cycle.

problemSet.problem: Derive the Euclidean distance from (I, A) to the line A + I = 1 without quoting the point-to-line formula (minimise over the points (t, 1 − t)). Evaluate it for the lab's domain module (I = 1/6, A = 0).
problemSet.solution: Squared distance f(t) = (I − t)² + (A − 1 + t)². f′(t) = −2(I − t) + 2(A − 1 + t) = 0 ⇒ t* = (I − A + 1)/2. Then I − t* = (I + A − 1)/2 and A − 1 + t* = (I + A − 1)/2, so f(t*) = (I + A − 1)²/2 and the distance is |I + A − 1|/√2. For domain: |1/6 − 1|/√2 = (5/6)/√2 ≈ 0.5893 – the value the lab's brute-force search printed.

problemSet.problem: 'Low coupling causes fewer defects, so we should gate merges on Martin's Dn.' Critically evaluate this claim in ≤ 600 words, using at least two empirical studies from the concept note.
problemSet.solution: A strong answer: (1) separates correlation from causation – Zimmermann & Nagappan (2008) found that network measures on dependency graphs predicted defect-prone Windows Server 2003 binaries with recall about 10 percentage points higher than complexity metrics, which supports dependency structure as a *predictor*, not as a lever; (2) raises confounding – El Emam et al. (2001) showed that after controlling for class size, the object-oriented metrics they studied were no longer associated with fault-proneness, so any coupling–defect claim must control for size; (3) notes external validity – single systems, specific languages; (4) notes Martin's own caveat that his metrics measure conformance to a pattern he believes is good; (5) proposes a proportionate use: track Dn and cycles as signals and ratchets (no new cycles; no new edges into unstable modules), review outliers, and do not treat a threshold as proof of quality. Marked with the lesson rubric.

"""Numerical checks for the lesson 23 theorems. Run: python check_modularity.py  (exit 0 = every check holds)."""
import math
import random
import sys

import modularity as m

FAILURES = []


def check(label, ok):
    print(f"  [{'OK' if ok else 'FAIL'}] {label}")
    if not ok:
        FAILURES.append(label)


def theorem_layering(rng, trials=2000):
    print("T1 strict layering <=> acyclic")
    strict_acyclic = sum(m.is_acyclic(*m.random_graph(rng, 12, 0.3, strict=True)[:2]) for _ in range(trials))
    check(f"{strict_acyclic}/{trials} random strictly layered graphs are acyclic", strict_acyclic == trials)
    loose_cyclic = sum(not m.is_acyclic(*m.random_graph(rng, 12, 0.3, strict=False)[:2]) for _ in range(trials))
    print(f"      (same-layer edges allowed: {loose_cyclic}/{trials} graphs have a cycle - strictness matters)")
    dags = violations = 0
    for _ in range(trials):
        order = list(range(12))
        rng.shuffle(order)
        pos = {v: k for k, v in enumerate(order)}
        edges = [(a, b) for a in order for b in order if pos[a] < pos[b] and rng.random() < 0.3]
        level = m.longest_path_layering(order, edges)
        dags += 1
        violations += len(m.strict_layering_violations(edges, level))
    check(f"converse: longest-path layering of {dags} random DAGs has {violations} violations", violations == 0)
    for name, lab in (("layered (L100 #2)", m.LAYERED), ("hexagonal (L200 #7)", m.HEXAGONAL)):
        nodes, edges, _ = m.module_graph(lab)
        level = m.longest_path_layering(nodes, edges)
        layers = {}
        for node, lv in sorted(level.items()):
            layers.setdefault(lv, []).append(node)
        check(f"{name}: {len(edges)} edges, acyclic, layers {dict(sorted(layers.items()))}",
              m.is_acyclic(nodes, edges) and not m.strict_layering_violations(edges, level))


def theorem_condensation(rng, trials=2000):
    print("T2 the condensation (SCC graph) of any directed graph is acyclic")
    ok = cyclic_inputs = 0
    for _ in range(trials):
        nodes = list(range(10))
        edges = [(a, b) for a in nodes for b in nodes if a != b and rng.random() < 0.15]
        cyclic_inputs += not m.is_acyclic(nodes, edges)
        cnodes, cedges, _ = m.condensation(nodes, edges)
        ok += m.is_acyclic(cnodes, cedges)
    check(f"{ok}/{trials} condensations acyclic ({cyclic_inputs} of the inputs had cycles)", ok == trials)
    nodes, with_main, _ = m.module_graph(m.HEXAGONAL, include_main=True)
    big = [sorted(c) for c in m.tarjan_scc(nodes, with_main) if len(c) > 1]
    check(f"hexagonal lab read WITH its __main__ blocks: cycle component {big} "
          f"(driving_cli's entry block imports app, app imports driving_cli)", big == [["app", "driving_cli"]])
    nodes, edges, _ = m.module_graph(m.HEXAGONAL)
    seeded = edges + [("domain", "driving_http")]  # seeded fault: the domain reaches out to an adapter
    big = [sorted(c) for c in m.tarjan_scc(nodes, seeded) if len(c) > 1]
    check(f"seeded edge domain -> driving_http creates the cycle component {big}",
          big == [["domain", "driving_http"]] and not m.is_acyclic(nodes, seeded))


def theorem_main_sequence():
    print("T3 Martin metrics on Library Loans (L200 #7 hexagonal): I, A in [0,1]; distance to A + I = 1 is Dn / sqrt(2)")
    nodes, edges, classes = m.module_graph(m.HEXAGONAL)
    rows = m.martin_metrics(nodes, edges, classes)
    print(f"      {'module':<14}{'Ca':>3}{'Ce':>3}{'I':>7}{'A':>6}{'Dn':>7}{'numeric d':>11}")
    worst = 0.0
    for name, r in rows.items():
        numeric = m.distance_to_main_sequence_numeric(r["A"], r["I"])
        worst = max(worst, abs(numeric - r["Dn"] / math.sqrt(2)))
        print(f"      {name:<14}{r['Ca']:>3}{r['Ce']:>3}{r['I']:>7.3f}{r['A']:>6.2f}{r['Dn']:>7.3f}{numeric:>11.4f}")
    check("all I and A in [0, 1]", all(0 <= r["I"] <= 1 and 0 <= r["A"] <= 1 for r in rows.values()))
    check(f"max |numeric distance - Dn/sqrt(2)| = {worst:.1e} (< 1e-5)", worst < 1e-5)
    mean_dn = sum(r["Dn"] for r in rows.values()) / len(rows)
    print(f"      mean Dn = {mean_dn:.3f}; furthest from the main sequence: "
          f"{max(rows, key=lambda n: rows[n]['Dn'])} (stable and concrete: the 'zone of pain' corner)")


def kwic_example():
    print("Worked example: Parnas KWIC change impact (modules that must change per design decision)")
    for label, knows in (("conventional", m.KWIC_CONVENTIONAL), ("information hiding", m.KWIC_HIDING)):
        impact = m.change_impact(knows)
        counts = [len(v) for v in impact.values()]
        print(f"      {label:<19} {counts} total {sum(counts)}, worst {max(counts)}")
    check("information hiding: every decision is known by exactly one module",
          all(len(v) == 1 for v in m.change_impact(m.KWIC_HIDING).values()))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    rng = random.Random(500)
    theorem_layering(rng)
    theorem_condensation(rng)
    theorem_main_sequence()
    kwic_example()
    print("ALL CHECKS OK" if not FAILURES else f"FAILED: {FAILURES}")
    sys.exit(1 if FAILURES else 0)

theorems.name: T24.1 Series composition and its bounds
theorems.statement: A service that needs all of n components, component i up with probability Aᵢ, has availability A = ∏Aᵢ if failures are independent. Without independence, 1 − Σ(1 − Aᵢ) ≤ A ≤ minᵢ Aᵢ.
theorems.proof:
Let Uᵢ be the event 'component i is up'. The service is up exactly on U₁ ∩ … ∩ Uₙ. With independence, P(∩Uᵢ) = ∏P(Uᵢ) = ∏Aᵢ. Upper bound: ∩Uᵢ ⊆ Uⱼ for every j, so P(∩Uᵢ) ≤ Aⱼ for all j, hence ≤ min Aᵢ. Lower bound: the complement is ∪Uᵢᶜ and by Boole's inequality P(∪Uᵢᶜ) ≤ ΣP(Uᵢᶜ) = Σ(1 − Aᵢ), so A ≥ 1 − Σ(1 − Aᵢ). ∎

Reading: a chain is never stronger than its weakest link, and with many links the unavailabilities roughly add – the 'rule of the extra 9' in Treynor et al. (2017).

theorems.name: T24.2 Parallel redundancy and k-of-n
theorems.statement: With independent replicas, the 'any one is enough' structure has A = 1 − ∏(1 − Aᵢ). For n identical replicas of availability a and a requirement of at least k up, A = Σ_{j=k..n} C(n, j) aʲ (1 − a)ⁿ⁻ʲ.
theorems.proof:
The parallel structure is down exactly when all replicas are down: P(∩Uᵢᶜ) = ∏(1 − Aᵢ) by independence; take the complement. For k-of-n, the number X of replicas up is a sum of n independent Bernoulli(a) variables, so X ~ Binomial(n, a) and P(X ≥ k) = Σ_{j ≥ k} C(n, j) aʲ(1 − a)ⁿ⁻ʲ. For k = 1 this equals 1 − (1 − a)ⁿ, the parallel formula. ∎

Caveat: common-mode failures (same bad deploy, same database, same region) break independence; then redundancy buys far less than the formula promises (problem P24-5).

theorems.name: T24.3 Nines, downtime and steady-state availability
theorems.statement: Over a period T the allowed downtime is (1 − A)·T, so each extra nine divides it by 10. If a component alternates i.i.d. up periods (mean MTTF) and repair periods (mean MTTR), the long-run fraction of time up is MTTF / (MTTF + MTTR), whatever the distributions.
theorems.proof: Downtime: by definition of the time-average availability. One more nine maps 1 − A to (1 − A)/10, so (1 − A)T is divided by 10. theorems.name: T24.4 Break-even weight between two options
theorems.statement: Two options x, y are scored on two criteria with weights (w, 1 − w). With d = x − y, the score difference Δ(w) = w·d₁ + (1 − w)·d₂ is affine, so there is at most one break-even weight w* = d₂ / (d₂ − d₁) in (0, 1); it exists iff d₁ and d₂ have opposite signs, and the preferred option flips there.
theorems.proof:
Δ(w) = d₂ + w(d₁ − d₂) is a line in w. If d₁ = d₂ it is constant (no flip). Otherwise its unique root is w* = d₂ / (d₂ − d₁). A line takes values Δ(0) = d₂ and Δ(1) = d₁ at the ends, so its root lies strictly inside (0, 1) iff d₂ and d₁ are non-zero with opposite signs; then Δ changes sign at w* and nowhere else. ∎

"""Numerical checks for the lesson 24 theorems. Run: python check_quality.py  (exit 0 = every check holds)."""
import itertools
import math
import random
import sys

import availability as av
import tradeoff as tr

FAILURES = []


def check(label, ok):
    print(f"  [{'OK' if ok else 'FAIL'}] {label}")
    if not ok:
        FAILURES.append(label)


def exact_by_enumeration(comps, structure):
    """Sum the probability of every up/down state in which the structure works (2^n states, exact)."""
    names, total = list(comps), 0.0
    for bits in itertools.product([True, False], repeat=len(names)):
        state = dict(zip(names, bits))
        if structure(state):
            total += math.prod(comps[n] if state[n] else 1 - comps[n] for n in names)
    return total


def theorem_series_parallel(rng):
    print("T1/T2 series = product, parallel = 1 - product of unavailabilities (independent components)")
    c = av.LIBRARY_LOANS
    comps = {"load balancer": c["load balancer"], "api 1": c["api instance"], "api 2": c["api instance"],
             "database": c["database"], "identity provider": c["identity provider"]}
    formula = av.library_loans(2)
    exact = exact_by_enumeration(comps, av.library_loans_structure)
    check(f"Library Loans (LB, 2 API replicas, DB, IdP): formula {formula:.6%} = enumeration of 32 states "
          f"{exact:.6%} (|diff| {abs(formula - exact):.1e})", abs(formula - exact) < 1e-12)
    trials = 400_000
    mc = av.monte_carlo(av.library_loans_structure, comps, trials, rng)
    sigma = math.sqrt(formula * (1 - formula) / trials)
    check(f"Monte Carlo {trials:,} trials: {mc:.4%} within 4 sigma ({4 * sigma:.4%}) of the formula",
          abs(mc - formula) < 4 * sigma)
    serial = [c["load balancer"], c["api instance"], c["database"], c["identity provider"]]
    a = av.series(serial)
    check(f"one API instance: series {a:.4%}; union bound {av.union_bound(serial):.4%} <= A <= min {min(serial):.2%}",
          av.union_bound(serial) <= a <= min(serial))
    print(f"      adding the 2nd API replica: {a:.4%} -> {formula:.4%}; a 3rd: {av.library_loans(3):.4%} "
          f"(the database is now the limit: {c['database']:.2%})")
    for k in (1, 2, 3):
        comps3 = {f"r{i}": 0.99 for i in range(3)}
        exact3 = exact_by_enumeration(comps3, lambda s, k=k: sum(s.values()) >= k)
        check(f"{k}-of-3 replicas at 99%: binomial {av.k_of_n(k, 3, 0.99):.6%} = enumeration {exact3:.6%}",
              abs(av.k_of_n(k, 3, 0.99) - exact3) < 1e-12)
    check("1-of-n equals parallel([a]*n)", abs(av.k_of_n(1, 3, 0.99) - av.parallel([0.99] * 3)) < 1e-15)


def theorem_nines(rng):
    print("T3 nines -> downtime, and steady-state availability = MTTF / (MTTF + MTTR)")
    print(f"      {'SLO':>8}{'min / 30 days':>15}{'h / year':>10}")
    table = av.nines_table()
    for a, month, year in table:
        print(f"      {a:>8.3%}{month:>15.2f}{year:>10.3f}")
    ratios = [table[i][2] / table[j][2] for i, j in ((0, 1), (1, 3), (3, 4))]
    check(f"each extra nine divides allowed downtime by 10: ratios {[round(r, 6) for r in ratios]}",
          all(abs(r - 10) < 1e-9 for r in ratios))
    budget = av.downtime_minutes(0.9999)
    check(f"CACM example: 3 outages x 20 min = 60 min > {budget:.2f} min allowed by 99.99%/year", 60 > budget)
    mttf, mttr = 720.0, 1.0
    formula = mttf / (mttf + mttr)
    for repair in ("exponential", "uniform"):
        sim = av.simulate_up_fraction(mttf, mttr, 20_000_000, rng, repair)
        check(f"MTTF 720 h, MTTR 1 h, {repair} repair: simulated up fraction {sim:.5%} vs formula {formula:.5%}",
              abs(sim - formula) < 2e-4)


def theorem_break_even(rng):
    print("T4 two criteria, weights (w, 1-w): at most one break-even weight w*; preference flips there")
    x, y = tr.SINGLE_SQLITE, tr.REPLICATED_POSTGRES
    w_star = tr.break_even(x, y)
    flips = [i / 10_000 for i in range(1, 10_001)
             if (tr.weighted_score(x, i / 10_000) > tr.weighted_score(y, i / 10_000)) !=
             (tr.weighted_score(x, (i - 1) / 10_000) > tr.weighted_score(y, (i - 1) / 10_000))]
    check(f"SQLite {x} vs replicated PostgreSQL {y}: w* = {w_star:.4f}; sweep flips at {flips}",
          len(flips) == 1 and abs(flips[0] - w_star) <= 1e-4)
    mismatches = 0
    for _ in range(2000):
        p, q = (rng.random(), rng.random()), (rng.random(), rng.random())
        grid = [tr.weighted_score(p, i / 1000) - tr.weighted_score(q, i / 1000) for i in range(1001)]
        sign_changes = sum(1 for a, b in zip(grid, grid[1:]) if (a > 0) != (b > 0))
        mismatches += sign_changes != (1 if tr.break_even(p, q) is not None else 0)
    check(f"2,000 random option pairs: sign changes match the formula ({mismatches} mismatches)", mismatches == 0)
    print("      utility tree, highest priority first (importance, difficulty):")
    for attr, _, scenario, imp, dif in tr.prioritise()[:3]:
        print(f"        ({imp},{dif}) {attr}: {scenario[:70]}...")


if __name__ == "__main__":

    theorem_series_parallel(rng)
    theorem_nines(rng)
    theorem_break_even(rng)

glossary.meaning: What the caller must guarantee before a call / what the operation guarantees after it (Hoare, Meyer's design by contract).
A predicate on an object's state that holds after construction and after every public operation.
A rejected operation leaves the state unchanged, so the invariant still holds.
S is a subtype of T if programs written against T's specification stay correct with S (Liskov & Wing 1994).
'Nothing bad ever happens' – violated by a finite trace, e.g. two active loans of one book.
Exhaustive exploration of a model's reachable states to verify a property or produce a counterexample trace.
Reachable states grow exponentially with the number of concurrent components (3ⁿ in the buggy model here).
A variable (e.g. size) that influences both a metric and the outcome, creating a spurious association.

conceptSummary: Contracts make 'correct' precise; invariants are proved by induction over operations; subtypes may only weaken preconditions and strengthen postconditions; a model checker turns a race into a 4-step trace; and the empirical evidence on modularity is real but correlational and easily confounded by size.

theorems.name: T25.1 Invariant induction for an aggregate
theorems.statement: Let Inv be a predicate on the state of an aggregate. If (i) Inv holds after construction, (ii) every public operation, started in a state satisfying Inv and its precondition, ends in a state satisfying Inv, and (iii) a rejected operation leaves the state unchanged, then Inv holds in every state reachable through the public API.
theorems.proof:
Induction on the number n of public calls. Base n = 0: the state is the constructed one; Inv holds by (i). Step: assume Inv holds in state sₙ. The next call either is rejected – by (iii) sₙ₊₁ = sₙ, so Inv holds – or proceeds with its precondition satisfied, and by (ii) sₙ₊₁ satisfies Inv. Hence Inv holds for all n. ∎

The hidden premise is encapsulation: 'reachable through the public API' must cover every way the state can change. If outside code can append to the internal list, the induction proves nothing – which is why the L200 #8 aggregate exposes loans as a read-only tuple. For Member, Inv = (|active| ≤ max_loans) ∧ (no book twice among active loans); borrow's precondition is |active| < max ∧ book ∉ active, which is exactly what its guard checks.

theorems.name: T25.2 Liskov substitution rule for a method
theorems.statement: Let T specify method m by (pre_T, post_T) and let S implement m with (pre_S, post_S). If pre_T ⇒ pre_S and (pre_T ∧ post_S) ⇒ post_T, then every client proved correct against T's specification remains correct when it receives an S. (Liskov & Wing 1994 also require invariants and history constraints to be preserved.)
theorems.proof:
Sketch. A client correct against T establishes pre_T before calling m and afterwards relies only on post_T. With an S: pre_T ⇒ pre_S, so S's implementation is called inside its own precondition and, being correct against its spec, establishes post_S. Since pre_T still holds about the call's inputs, pre_T ∧ post_S ⇒ post_T, so everything the client relied on still holds and its proof goes through unchanged. ∎ Full treatment (with invariants, history rule and the two subtype definitions): Liskov & Wing (1994).

Contrapositive used by the check: a subtype that refuses inputs T accepts (stronger precondition) or returns results T forbids (weaker postcondition) can break some correct client – and the lab exhibits one.

theorems.name: T25.3 BFS model checking is complete for finite models and returns shortest counterexamples
theorems.statement: For a finite transition system, breadth-first search from the initial state visits exactly the reachable states and terminates. If an unsafe state is reachable, the first unsafe state BFS dequeues has minimal distance from the start, so following parent pointers gives a shortest counterexample trace.
theorems.proof:
Each state is enqueued at most once (the parent map is checked first), and only successors of visited states are enqueued, so BFS visits a subset of the reachable states and terminates after at most |S| dequeues. Conversely every reachable state at distance d is enqueued by the time the states at distance d − 1 are expanded (induction on d), so all reachable states are visited. Standard BFS lemma: states leave the queue in non-decreasing distance order; hence the first unsafe state dequeued has the minimum distance among unsafe states, and its parent chain has exactly that many steps. ∎

Limits: the result is about the *model*, not the code; the model must be finite (bounded members, books, operations); and state counts grow exponentially (3ⁿ for the buggy model, (n + 2)·2ⁿ⁻¹ for the fixed one).

problemSet.problem: For the L200 #8 Member aggregate, prove that borrow preserves Inv = (|active| ≤ max) ∧ (active book ids are distinct), given that borrow raises without changing state unless |active| < max and the book is not already active.
problemSet.solution: Assume Inv in state s. Case 1, the guard fails: an exception is raised before any mutation, so s′ = s and Inv holds. Case 2, the guard passes: |active| < max and b ∉ active. borrow appends one new active loan of b, so |active′| = |active| + 1 ≤ max, and active′ = active ∪ {b} with b new, so ids stay distinct. Both conjuncts hold; with the same argument for give_back (which only marks a loan returned) T25.1 gives Inv everywhere.

problemSet.problem: Write the precondition and postcondition of Member.give_back(book_id, today) as predicates on the state.
problemSet.solution: pre: ∃ an active loan with book_id (else NotBorrowed is raised and the state is unchanged). post: that loan now has returned_on = today; |active′| = |active| − 1; book_id ∉ active′; all other loans unchanged; Inv holds.

problemSet.problem: Supertype LoanLimit.allowed(active, overdue) has pre_T: 0 ≤ active ≤ 10, 0 ≤ overdue ≤ 3; post_T: result ⇒ active < 3, and (active = 0 ∧ overdue = 0) ⇒ result. Decide, with justification, whether each is a behavioural subtype: StrictLimit (active < 2 ∧ overdue = 0), GenerousLimit (active < 5), NoOverdueAccepted (raises if overdue > 0, else active < 3).
problemSet.solution: StrictLimit: same precondition; result ⇒ active < 2 < 3 and the new-member case returns True, so post_S ⇒ post_T: a subtype. GenerousLimit: returns True at active = 3, 4, violating result ⇒ active < 3: postcondition weakened, not a subtype (a client relying on 'never more than 3' borrows 5). NoOverdueAccepted: refuses inputs with overdue > 0 that pre_T admits: precondition strengthened, not a subtype (a supertype client gets an exception). The lab counts 0/0, 0/8 and 33/0 violating points.

problemSet.problem: On the same 44-point domain, how many points violate the precondition rule and how many the postcondition rule for an implementation that returns active < 4?
problemSet.numericAnswer: post broken at 4 of 44 points, pre at 0
problemSet.solution: It accepts every input (pre at 0). It returns True at active = 3 for overdue 0..3, breaking result ⇒ active < 3: 4 points. Result: post broken at 4 of 44 points, pre at 0. Recomputed by research/l500_checks.py.

problemSet.problem: Run the BFS model checker on the two-member workflow. How long is the shortest counterexample for the buggy check-then-act version, and how many reachable states do the buggy and fixed models have?
problemSet.solution: Shortest trace: A reads (free), B reads (free), A borrows, B borrows – both hold the book. Buggy model: each member is in one of 3 local states and the loans set is determined by them: 3² = 9. Fixed model: 8 (no state with two holders). Result: 4 steps; 9 and 8 reachable states.

problemSet.problem: Derive the number of reachable states of the fixed model with n members, and of the buggy model, and compare for n = 2..6.
problemSet.solution: Buggy: every combination of local states (idle, checked, holding) is reachable and the loans set equals the set of holders, so 3ⁿ. Fixed: at most one holder. No holder: each member idle or checked, 2ⁿ states. One holder: n choices, the others idle or checked, n·2ⁿ⁻¹. Total 2ⁿ + n·2ⁿ⁻¹ = (n + 2)·2ⁿ⁻¹. Result: fixed 8, 20, 48, 112, 256; buggy 9, 27, 81, 243, 729. Both grow exponentially (state explosion) – real model checkers use symmetry and partial-order reduction (not covered here).

problemSet.problem: The fixed model is safe. List three reasons why this does not prove that the production Library Loans service cannot lend one book twice, and say what you would do about each.
problemSet.solution: (1) Model–code gap: the model abstracts the code; keep them linked with a test that runs the counterexample schedule against the real repository (two threads, deterministic interleaving). (2) Bounded model: one book, n members, no crashes or retries; extend the model with a crash between read and insert, or use a tool such as TLA+ for larger bounds. (3) The 'atomic conditional insert' is an assumption about the database; enforce it with a unique constraint on active loans per book and test it against the real engine (Testcontainers in L200 #11).

problemSet.problem: Does modular design reduce defects? Evaluate the evidence from Zimmermann & Nagappan (2008), El Emam et al. (2001) and MacCormack et al. (2006) in ≤ 700 words: what each study measured, what it found, what it cannot show, and what an architect may honestly claim to stakeholders.
problemSet.solution: Model answer outline: Zimmermann & Nagappan – dependency-graph network measures on Windows Server 2003 binaries predicted defect-prone binaries better than complexity metrics (recall about 10 points higher) and found 60 % of the binaries developers considered critical; observational, one system, prediction ≠ causation. El Emam et al. – after controlling for class size, the OO metrics studied lost their association with fault-proneness in a large C++ framework: size is a confounder, many earlier 'validations' are suspect. MacCormack et al. – DSM-based metrics showed Linux more modular than the first Mozilla release and a deliberate redesign made Mozilla more modular; it is about structure and organisation, not defects, and is exploratory. Honest claim: dependency structure is associated with where defects and change costs concentrate; we use it to focus review and testing and to keep change local, and we measure outcomes (defects, lead time) rather than promise them. Marked with the rubric.

"""Numerical checks for the lesson 25 theorems. Run: python check_formal.py  (exit 0 = every check holds)."""
import random
import sys

import contracts as c
import model_check as mc

FAILURES = []


def check(label, ok):
    print(f"  [{'OK' if ok else 'FAIL'}] {label}")
    if not ok:
        FAILURES.append(label)


def theorem_invariant(rng):
    print("T1 invariant induction: Inv(initial) and every operation preserves Inv => Inv in every reachable state")
    check("base case: a new Member satisfies Inv", c.invariant(c.Member("m0")))
    s = c.random_traces(rng)
    print(f"      {s['calls']:,} random calls on the real L200 #8 Member aggregate, {s['rejected']:,} rejected by rules")
    check(f"Inv broken after {s['inv_broken']} calls", s["inv_broken"] == 0)
    check(f"borrow postcondition broken {s['post_broken']} times", s["post_broken"] == 0)
    check(f"rejected calls that changed state: {s['not_atomic']}", s["not_atomic"] == 0)
    check("loans is exposed as a read-only tuple (no append behind the root's back)",
          isinstance(c.Member("m9").loans, tuple))


def theorem_liskov():
    print("T2 Liskov rule: weaker-or-equal precondition and stronger-or-equal postcondition => safe substitution")
    expected = {"StrictLimit": (0, 0), "GenerousLimit": (0, 8), "NoOverdueAccepted": (33, 0)}
    for impl in (c.StrictLimit(), c.GenerousLimit(), c.NoOverdueAccepted()):
        name = type(impl).__name__
        pre_b, post_b = c.substitution_violations(impl)
        outcome = [c.client_borrow_up_to_limit(impl, overdue) for overdue in (0, 1)]
        print(f"      {name:<18} pre broken at {pre_b:>2} of {len(c.DOMAIN)} points, post broken at {post_b:>2}; "
              f"supertype client (overdue 0 / 1) ends with: {outcome}")
        check(f"{name}: violations {(pre_b, post_b)} as predicted {expected[name]}", (pre_b, post_b) == expected[name])
    check("the client written for the supertype stays within 3 loans only with the valid subtype",
          c.client_borrow_up_to_limit(c.StrictLimit()) <= 3 and c.client_borrow_up_to_limit(c.GenerousLimit()) > 3)


def theorem_model_checking():
    print("T3 BFS model checking: explores every reachable state; the first violation found has a shortest trace")
    n_bug, cex, _, _ = mc.bfs(fixed=False)
    brute = mc.shortest_by_enumeration(fixed=False)
    print(f"      buggy check-then-act: violation after exploring {n_bug} states; counterexample: {cex}")
    check(f"BFS counterexample length {len(cex)} = brute-force minimum {brute}", cex is not None and len(cex) == brute)
    n_fix, cex_fix, dead, _ = mc.bfs(fixed=True)
    check(f"atomic conditional insert: {n_fix} reachable states, no violation, {len(dead)} deadlocks",
          cex_fix is None and not dead and mc.shortest_by_enumeration(fixed=True) is None)
    ok, n = mc.can_always_free_book(fixed=True)
    check(f"AG EF book available: from all {n} reachable states the book can become free again", ok)
    counts = {k: (mc.reachable_states(False, tuple("ABCDEF"[:k])), mc.reachable_states(True, tuple("ABCDEF"[:k])))
              for k in range(2, 7)}
    print(f"      state explosion, members -> (buggy, fixed) reachable states: {counts}")
    check("buggy = 3^n and fixed = (n + 2) * 2^(n - 1) for n = 2..6",
          all(b == 3 ** k and f == (k + 2) * 2 ** (k - 1) for k, (b, f) in counts.items()))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    theorem_invariant(random.Random(2500))
    theorem_liskov()
    theorem_model_checking()
    print("ALL CHECKS OK" if not FAILURES else f"FAILED: {FAILURES}")
    sys.exit(1 if FAILURES else 0)

title: Ethics and professional responsibility: accessibility, privacy by design and honest technical debt
description: Accessibility (WCAG 2.2) and privacy by design (GDPR Art. 25) treated as architectural requirements, technical debt as a duty of honest disclosure, and a structured analysis of a Library Loans launch using the ACM Code.
outcome: You can identify stakeholders and harms, map a design decision to the ACM Code, WCAG 2.2 and GDPR Art. 25, argue for a defensible option, and write an honest status report and debt register for decision makers.
environment: No code. Reading, discussion, written case analysis.
estimatedTime: 4 hours (reading 1.5 h, seminar 1 h, written analysis 1.5 h)
prerequisites: Lesson 10 (authentication) and lesson 18 (multi-tenancy) for the technical context
No legal background assumed; this lesson is not legal advice
learningObjectives: Explain why accessibility and privacy are architectural (cross-cutting, costly to retrofit) rather than UI or legal afterthoughts.
Analyze a launch decision with a structured method: facts, stakeholders, harms, options, principles, recommendation.
Evaluate options against the ACM Code (1.2, 1.3, 1.4, 1.6, 2.5, 3.1), WCAG 2.2 success criteria and GDPR Art. 25.
Critique a status report for misleading claims and rewrite it with an honest technical-debt register.

glossary.meaning: A, AA or AAA; AA is the level most laws and policies reference. WCAG 2.2 adds 9 success criteria to 2.1 and removes 4.1.1 Parsing.
A new WCAG 2.2 AA criterion: sign-in must not depend on a cognitive function test (e.g. a puzzle) unless an alternative or assistance is provided.

glossary.term: data protection by design / by default
glossary.meaning: GDPR Art. 25: appropriate technical and organisational measures from design time; by default only the personal data necessary for each purpose are processed.
Collect and keep only what each purpose needs – named in Art. 25(1) as a principle the measures must implement.
Cunningham (1992): shipping not-quite-right code is like borrowing; the interest is the extra cost paid until it is repaid.
A public claim about which standard and level a product meets; a false claim is a misrepresentation (ACM 1.3).

conceptSummary: Accessibility and privacy are quality attributes with legal teeth; they must be scenarios in the utility tree, not a launch-week checklist. Debt is legitimate only when it is disclosed, owned and dated; claiming compliance you do not have is dishonest, not an engineering trade-off.

caseStudy.case: Library Loans goes public. A city's library network will open online borrowing in two weeks. An internal audit finds three WCAG 2.2 AA failures in the borrow flow: the sign-in page relies on a distorted-text puzzle (SC 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum)), reading lists can only be reordered by dragging (SC 2.5.7 Dragging Movements), and the 'renew' buttons are tiny icons (SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum)). Fixing them needs about three weeks because the sign-in page belongs to a third-party identity component. Separately, the analytics team wants full loan histories kept indefinitely and enabled by default 'to train recommendations'. The product owner asks you, the architect, to tell the city council that the service is 'WCAG 2.2 AA compliant and privacy by design' and to log the remaining work as 'minor tech debt'. Two real precedents frame the stakes: in Robles v. Domino's (9th Cir. 2019) the court held that the ADA applied to a pizza chain's website and app; in November 2022 the Irish DPC fined Meta €265 million for infringing GDPR Articles 25(1) and 25(2) (data protection by design and by default).
stakeholders: Members who are blind or have low vision, motor or cognitive disabilities, and older members
All other members, including children and their parents
Library staff who handle complaints and paper fallbacks
City council (funder, legally responsible public body) and its data protection officer
Product owner and delivery team (deadline, reputation)
Architect / developers (professional duties under the ACM Code)
Analytics team and any recommendation vendor
Regulators and courts (data protection authority, equality / accessibility enforcement)
Disability advocacy groups and the wider public (trust in a public service)
questions: Which facts are established, which are assumptions, and which need a lawyer or the DPO to answer?
Who is harmed, how badly and how reversibly, by each of: launching as is; delaying three weeks; launching with an accessible alternative path?
Is the requested statement to the council true? Which ACM principles does it engage, and what would an honest statement say?
What should the default retention of loan history be under GDPR Art. 25(2), and what architecture implements it?
How should accessibility and privacy appear in the utility tree and fitness functions so this does not recur?
When is technical debt ethically acceptable, and what makes 'minor tech debt' a misleading label here?
frameworks: ACM Code of Ethics 2018: 1.2 Avoid harm; 1.3 Be honest and trustworthy; 1.4 Be fair and take action not to discriminate (failure to design for accessibility may be unfair discrimination); 1.6 Respect privacy (minimum data, defined retention); 2.5 Give comprehensive and thorough evaluations … including analysis of possible risks; 3.1 public good; 3.7 systems integrated into the infrastructure of society.
Software Engineering Code of Ethics 5.2 (ACM/IEEE-CS): principles 1 PUBLIC, 3 PRODUCT, 4 JUDGMENT.
GDPR Art. 25(1) by design and 25(2) by default; Irish DPC Meta decision (2022) as an enforcement example.
ALA Privacy interpretation of the Library Bill of Rights: circulation records are confidential; retain the minimum, anonymise when possible.
Cunningham's debt metaphor: debt is acceptable when it is repaid promptly; interest accrues while it is not.
caseStudy.modelAnswer: 1 Facts and uncertainty. Established: three AA failures in the core flow; ~3 weeks to fix; analytics wants indefinite, default-on history. Uncertain: which laws apply to this city (ask the DPO / legal; the EAA's scope may not cover a public library service; national public-sector accessibility rules may). 2 Harms. Launch as is: blind and motor-impaired members are excluded from a public service at launch (severe for them, reversible only by the fix), plus legal and reputational risk; indefinite default-on histories expose what people read – a classic chilling effect libraries exist to prevent – and enlarge breach impact. 3 Options. (A) Launch and claim compliance: rejected – the claim is false (ACM 1.3: no deliberately false or misleading claims; SE Code 3). (B) Delay three weeks: honest and inclusive, costs the deadline. (C) Launch on time with an equivalent accessible path (staff-assisted or alternative sign-in that satisfies 3.3.8, keyboard reorder controls, larger targets in a hotfix), publish a truthful conformance statement listing known failures and dates, and keep (B) as the fallback if the alternative path is not equivalent. 4 Privacy by design. Default: keep only active loans; delete or anonymise history N days after return; history for recommendations is opt-in, purpose-specific and revocable; analytics gets aggregates or pseudonymised data with the key held separately (Art. 25(1) names pseudonymisation and data minimisation; 25(2) limits default processing). Architecture: a retention job with a fitness function that fails CI if any table holds returned-loan rows older than N days; a policy check (L400 #19) that blocks analytics reads of member identifiers. 5 Recommendation and communication. Choose C if the DPO and an accessibility tester confirm the alternative path is equivalent, else B. Tell the council exactly what is true: 'The borrow flow does not yet meet WCAG 2.2 AA (3 criteria, listed); an accessible alternative is available; full conformance by <date>; loan history is not retained by default.' Record the work in a debt register with owner, interest (who is excluded meanwhile), and repayment date – it is not 'minor'. If the product owner insists on the false statement, escalate (ACM 1.2/2.5 duty to report risks) before going outside the organisation. 6 Prevention. Add inclusivity and privacy scenarios to the utility tree as (H, M), make them release gates, and buy or build identity components that meet SC 3.3.8.

problemSet.problem: Name the three WCAG 2.2 success criteria in the case, their level, and one concrete design change for each.
problemSet.solution: SC 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum), AA – support password managers/paste or passkeys, no puzzle without an alternative. SC 2.5.7 Dragging Movements, AA – add 'move up/down' buttons. SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum), AA – make targets at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels or spaced (check the normative text for exceptions).

problemSet.problem: Rewrite the product owner's statement to the council so that it is honest, specific and still useful.
problemSet.solution: 'Online borrowing launches on <date>. Three parts of the borrow flow do not yet meet WCAG 2.2 level AA (sign-in puzzle, drag-only reordering, small renew buttons); an accessible alternative is available from day one and full conformance is planned for <date>, owner <name>. Loan history is deleted 30 days after return unless a member opts in.' It states the standard, level, gaps, mitigation, date and owner (ACM 1.3, 2.5).

problemSet.problem: Design a privacy-by-default data flow for loan history that still allows a recommendation feature. Name the GDPR Art. 25 elements you implement.
problemSet.solution: Default: active loans only; returned loans deleted/anonymised after N days (25(2): only necessary data, limited storage period). Opt-in 'remember my history' per member, revocable, purpose-limited to recommendations. Recommender reads pseudonymised events (key held by the loans service) or aggregates (25(1): pseudonymisation, data minimisation). Enforce with a retention fitness function and access policy tests.

problemSet.problem: Write the structured case analysis (≤ 900 words): facts, stakeholders, harms, options, principles, recommendation, communication plan.
problemSet.solution: See the caseStudy modelAnswer; marked with the lesson rubric. Full marks need explicit uncertainty (what needs legal/DPO input), at least three options, correct use of ACM principles by number, and a communication plan that is true.

problemSet.problem: When is taking on technical debt ethically acceptable? Give two conditions and one counter-example from the case.
problemSet.solution: Acceptable when (1) the people who bear the interest know and agree (disclosed, owned, dated) and (2) the interest does not fall on people who cannot consent and are seriously harmed. Counter-example: labelling inaccessible sign-in as 'minor tech debt' moves the interest onto disabled members who were not asked.

problemSet.problem: Explain, with the lesson 24 vocabulary, why accessibility is an architectural concern and not only a UI task.
problemSet.solution: It is a quality attribute (ISO/IEC 25010:2023 interaction capability, subcharacteristic inclusivity) whose response depends on structural choices – the identity provider, component library, client rendering, how errors and status messages flow – that are expensive to change late. It belongs in the utility tree as a measurable scenario and in release gates.

problemSet.problem: Write the critical response for reading 1 (Parnas).
problemSet.solution: Marked with the rubric: a clear thesis; accurate paraphrase of Parnas (criterion, KWIC comparison, efficiency remark); a counter-argument (team ownership, Conway's law, deployment independence) considered fairly; a Library Loans example (e.g. the fines rules hidden behind the strangler facade in L400 #17); references.

problemSet.problem: Write the critical response for reading 2 (ATAM).
problemSet.solution: Marked with the rubric: accurate account of ATAM's purpose (risk identification, not precise prediction), steps and outputs; a concrete lightweight variant (utility tree kept in the repo, scenarios as tests, risks as ADR consequences, fitness functions instead of one-off analysis); limits acknowledged (stakeholder breadth is the part automation cannot replace).

problemSet.problem: Explain why you must summarise rather than reproduce these sources, and how you would quote correctly if needed.
problemSet.solution: Both are copyrighted (ACM; Carnegie Mellon University); free access is not a licence to republish. Use short quotations only where the exact words matter, in quotation marks with author, year and page or section, and otherwise paraphrase with a citation (ACM Code 1.5: credit creators, respect copyright).
